title: The 60-Second Scan
hook: Sixty seconds of structured looking beats an hour of staring, because attention finds what it is told to find and quietly drops the rest.
why:
You walk into a crowded kitchen at a party. Within a second your eyes go to the person you came to see, then to the loudest laugh, then to whoever is holding the food. That is attention doing its job: going to what is salient and to what you care about. An hour later you learn that a friend was standing by the back door the whole time, alone and miserable, and you never registered him, though he was in plain view for the entire evening.

Unstructured looking finds what it expects. A short, fixed routine of looking does something different: it sends your attention to places it would not go on its own, in an order that covers the room before it settles on anyone. It also ends. Sixty seconds of deliberate scanning followed by ordinary, relaxed presence is more perceptive, and far less strange to be around, than a man who watches everyone all evening. This chapter gives you the routine.

teach.h: Attention sees what it is aimed at, and misses what it is not.
teach.p:
In 1999 Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris asked people to watch a short film of two teams passing basketballs and to count the passes made by one team. Partway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the middle of the game, faced the camera, thumped their chest and walked off. About half of the viewers never saw it. They were not careless; they were doing exactly what they had been asked, and the task consumed the attention that would have noticed the gorilla.

Psychologists call this inattentional blindness, and it has been found again and again since Arien Mack and Irvin Rock gave it a name. It is not a quirk of laboratory films. It is how attention works everywhere: what you are looking for, and what you already care about, decide what reaches awareness. Everything else can pass through your visual field unrecorded.

For a reader of people this is humbling. When you walk into a room looking for your boss's mood, you will see your boss's mood and very little else. When you are worried about one friend, the other friend's trouble can stand two metres away without ever registering.

You cannot escape the limits of attention, but you can aim it deliberately. A routine scan is a way of telling attention, in advance, to visit places it would otherwise skip. It does not make you see everything. It makes you see more than your interests would have shown you, and it makes the gaps predictable rather than random.
teach.disconfirm: If, after running a structured scan for a few weeks, you find it never shows you anything your ordinary glance did not, your ordinary glance may already be broad. Test it by writing down what you noticed before and after scanning the same room.
teach.pullQuote: What you are looking for decides what reaches you.

teach.h: Scan in a fixed order: yourself, the room, the groups, one person.
teach.p:
The scan has four beats, each about fifteen seconds, always in the same order.

*Yourself.* Breath, shoulders, jaw, what you want from this room. The first chapter of this book explained why: your state colours everything that follows, and you will not notice it later.

*The room.* Layout, exits, light, noise, where the space pushes people. A narrow hallway crowds bodies together; a loud bar makes everyone lean in; a cold office keeps arms folded. The room explains a great deal of the behaviour in it before any person does.

*The groups.* Who is with whom, how tightly, which way the groups face. Who is on their own. Where attention seems to be flowing: toward a speaker, a screen, a door, a particular person.

*One person.* Only now do you let your attention settle, either on the person you came to see or on whoever the previous beat showed you was the exception. You give them your full attention for a few seconds, then let the scan end.

The order matters more than the timing. Starting with a person, as almost everyone does, lets that person absorb the whole minute. Starting with yourself and the room means that by the time you look at anyone, you already know what the setting is doing to everyone in it, and you are far less likely to read the room's effects as one person's feelings.
teach.disconfirm: If running the beats in a different order gives you the same picture of a room, the order may matter less for you than it does for most people. Try it both ways in a few places before deciding.

teach.h: Read each person from the ground up.
teach.p:
When the scan reaches people, sweep each one from the floor upward: feet and legs, then hands, then the orientation of the torso, then shoulders, then head, and the face last.

There are two reasons for this order. The first is the gradient of control from the chapter on leakage: the feet and legs are the least managed parts of most people's bodies, and the face the most. Starting at the bottom gives you the less curated signal first. The second reason is that faces capture attention more readily than almost anything else in a scene. If you start with a face, it tends to hold you, and the rest of the body never gets examined.

In practice, ground-up reading takes two or three seconds per person and catches things a face-first glance will miss: the man laughing at a joke while his feet point at the door, the woman nodding along whose hands have gone still, the colleague whose torso has turned a quarter away from the conversation he appears to be in.

None of these is a conclusion, as earlier chapters made clear. Feet pointing at a door may mean a wish to leave, a need for the bathroom or simply where the floor space is. What the ground-up sweep gives you is a fuller description to hold against this person's baseline, and occasionally a mismatch between top and bottom that is worth a second look.
teach.disconfirm: If, across many scans, the lower body never adds anything to what the face already told you, the sweep is not earning its seconds in your setting. Keep it, but note whether that changes in rooms where people are trying harder to look composed.

teach.h: Look for the exception, not the most interesting person.
teach.p:
Visual search research gives a useful hint about what to look for. In Anne Treisman's work on attention, a single item that differs from everything around it in one simple feature, a red dot among green ones, seems to pop out without effort, while finding an item defined by a combination of features requires slow, deliberate search.

Rooms work similarly. The most useful thing a scan can find is usually a simple difference from the room's pattern: the still person in a moving crowd, the one facing a different way from everyone else, the one standing outside every group, the one who is quiet in a loud room or loud in a quiet one. These differences tend to pop out once you know to look for them.

What a scan should not do is go straight to the most interesting person: the attractive one, the important one, the one you are worried about. Your interest will find them anyway. The scan's job is to find what your interest would miss.

An exception is not automatically a problem. The person standing alone may be the host taking a breather, someone waiting for a friend, or a person who simply likes the edges of rooms. The exception is where your attention goes next, gently and briefly, not where your conclusions go.

Absence counts as an exception too, and it is the one scans miss most often because there is nothing to see. The colleague who always sits by the window and today is not in the room; the friend who usually arrives first and has not come; the group that normally includes four people and today has three. A scan that only looks at who is present cannot find who is missing, so add one quiet question to the groups beat: who would I expect to see here?
teach.disconfirm: If the exceptions your scans pick out turn out, again and again, to have ordinary explanations you could not have helped with, the exceptions are not telling you much in that setting. That is useful to know; it tells you the room was fine.

teach.h: Use soft eyes, and honour civil inattention.
teach.p:
A scan done with a hard, fixed stare is both less effective and more intrusive than one done with soft eyes: a relaxed gaze that rests lightly on a point and takes in movement and shape at the edges of vision. Peripheral vision is poor at detail but good at motion and orientation, which is most of what a scan needs.

The sociologist Erving Goffman described the ordinary courtesy that strangers extend to each other in public as civil inattention: a brief glance that acknowledges the other person's presence, followed by a withdrawal of attention that signals they are not an object of special interest. Most people perform it dozens of times a day without noticing. Staring breaks it, and people feel the break immediately.

A good scan stays inside the rules of civil inattention. Glance, take in, move on. Return, if you need to, with another brief glance rather than a held look. If someone catches your eye, acknowledge it the way anyone would, with a small nod or a half-smile, and look elsewhere.

This matters for accuracy as well as manners. A person who feels watched changes their behaviour, as the chapter on baselines explained, and the change you then observe is one you caused. Soft, brief attention leaves the room as you found it.

The exact rules vary. How long a glance may last before it becomes a stare differs between cultures, between cities and countryside, and between a busy street and a quiet waiting room. When you are somewhere unfamiliar, watch how long other people let their eyes rest on strangers, and stay a little under it.
teach.disconfirm: If people around you start returning your gaze, shifting away or looking uncomfortable while you scan, your attention is landing harder than you think. Shorten the glances until no one reacts.

teach.h: End the scan with one question, then stop scanning.
teach.p:
A scan that never ends is not perception; it is vigilance. Constantly sweeping a room for threats or signals is tiring, unsettling to the people around you, and narrows over time into a search for danger. People who have been through trauma sometimes find themselves unable to stop scanning; that is a hard state to live in, not a skill to cultivate.

So the scan has an output and an end. The output is a single question or a single small action. *Is my cousin by the fence on his own because he wants to be?* *The meeting is tense around the projector; I'll wait before raising my item.* *The man at the end of the table hasn't spoken; I'll ask him directly.* Then you stop scanning and simply take part in the room.

You may run another scan later, when something changes: a new person arrives, the mood shifts, you move to a different room. In a long evening, three or four scans are plenty. Between them, your attention belongs to the people you are actually with.

The rhythm, a short deliberate look and then ordinary presence, is what separates a perceptive person from a watchful one. Others can relax around the first. Nobody relaxes around the second.

If the question was worth asking, it is worth a line in the journal that evening: what the scan showed, what you did, what happened. Over weeks those lines will show you whether your scans find things that matter or only things that are unusual, which are not the same.
teach.disconfirm: If you notice you cannot stop scanning, that every room makes you sweep and re-sweep, treat that as information about your own state rather than as diligence. The chapters on stress and on reading yourself under pressure are the place to start.

teach.h: Practise until it costs nothing, and know who the scan is for.
teach.p:
At first the scan will feel slow and self-conscious. Tie it to transitions you already make: walking into a room, sitting down at a table, joining a call. Run it at every transition for two weeks and it will begin to happen in well under a minute, with no sense of effort. That is when it becomes useful, because a skill that requires effort is abandoned the moment you are busy.

There is one more thing to be clear about. The ability to sweep a room and pick out the person who stands apart is not morally neutral. In a study often cited in self-defence courses, Betty Grayson and Morris Stein showed short films of pedestrians to men in prison for violent assaults and asked who would make an easy victim. Their choices were associated with features of the walkers' gait, such as stride and the way they moved their arms. People who prey on others scan rooms too.

This book teaches the scan for the opposite purpose: to notice the person who is struggling, excluded, unwell or afraid, so that you can help or give them room. If you ever catch yourself scanning a bar for someone who looks easy to approach, easy to persuade or easy to intimidate, you are using the same eyes for something this book refuses to teach.

The question at the end of every scan should be some version of the same one: who here could use something from me?
teach.disconfirm: If a month of daily scanning has not made the routine faster or more automatic, it may be attached to the wrong moments. Move it to a transition you never skip, such as sitting down, and try again.
teach.pullQuote: The question at the end of every scan is who here could use something from me.

poseGallery.doCaption: Sweeping in a set order, glancing and moving on.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Fixing on the most interesting person in the room.
poseGallery.annotation: Your interest will find the interesting people anyway. The scan exists to show you what your interest would skip.

poseGallery.doCaption: Soft eyes, the room taken in from the edges.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Watching one person until they feel it.
poseGallery.annotation: Peripheral vision is poor at detail but good at movement and orientation, which is most of what a scan needs.

poseGallery.doCaption: Scanning from a settled body, then letting the scan go.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Scanning braced, like a guard on duty.
poseGallery.annotation: A scan that never ends is vigilance, not perception. Look deliberately, then return to the room.

poseGallery.doCaption: Starting from the feet, which here point at the door.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Starting with the face, the channel people manage best.
poseGallery.annotation: Read each person from the ground up. Faces hold attention so readily that the rest of the body never gets a look.

poseGallery.doCaption: Scan done, back in the conversation
poseGallery.dontCaption: Scanning the party over a friend's shoulder
poseGallery.annotation: A scan that never ends turns a host into a guard. Run it, act on it, and then join the room.

poseGallery.doCaption: Slowing at the door for sixty seconds
poseGallery.dontCaption: Rushing into a room without a look
poseGallery.annotation: A minute at the threshold, in a fixed order, finds more than an hour of staring once you are inside.

caseStudy:
Joe has coached an under-twelves football team on Saturday mornings for three seasons. His assistant, Craig, is a former semi-professional player with a sharp eye for talent. Both men watch the boys closely, but they watch differently.

One October morning Joe runs his scan as he walks from the car park. Himself: rushed, a little irritable after a late night. The pitch: wet, cold wind from the north, parents clustered by the gate to keep warm. The groups: the usual knot of boys kicking a ball against the fence, two pairs doing keepy-uppies, a few still with their parents. The exception: Theo, normally one of the noisiest, standing on his own by the corner flag with his hood up, hands in his sleeves, facing away from the others.

Craig, watching the same scene, sees who is sharp in the warm-up and who is slow off the mark. When Theo misplaces three passes he notes it and moves him to the second group.

Joe treats the exception as a question, not a verdict. Cold and tired is the obvious rival explanation; it is a raw morning. So rather than asking Theo what is wrong, he gives him a job, setting out the cones with him, and talks about nothing much while they do it. Theo says almost nothing, then mentions that his dad is not coming to watch any more because he has moved out.

Joe does not dig. He tells Theo he is glad he came, keeps him in his usual group, and at pick-up tells Theo's mother only that Theo seemed quieter than usual and that he had enjoyed setting up with him. She thanks him and says it has been a hard month.

Over the next few weeks Theo arrives a little earlier each Saturday and starts helping with the cones without being asked. Craig, still watching for talent, never learns why.
observe: The next time you walk into a café, office or waiting room, run the four beats before you sit down: yourself, the room, the groups, one person. Afterwards, write down anything you saw that you would normally have missed.
At a gathering this week, run a scan once every half hour and notice only who is standing or sitting apart from any group. Note whether it is the same person each time.
On a bus or train, rest your gaze on a neutral point for five minutes and notice how much movement and orientation you can still read at the edges of your vision without looking directly at anyone.

drills.name: Count and Miss
steps: Find a short video of a busy public scene, such as a station concourse or a street market.
Watch it once while counting one specific thing, such as how many people look at their phones.
Watch it again with no task, simply taking in the scene.
List everything you noticed on the second viewing that you missed on the first.
Write one sentence about what your task made you blind to.
variations: Try the drill with a task of your own choosing in a real place, such as counting red coats on a high street, and then look again without the task.
Do the drill with a friend, each counting something different, and compare what each of you missed.
Watch a short clip of your own workplace or family gathering, if you have one, and notice what you missed while it was happening.

drills.name: Four Beats
steps: Choose three different public spaces you will pass through today.
In each, stand or sit for one minute and run the four beats in order: yourself, the room, the groups, one person.
Immediately afterwards, write one line for each beat.
Compare the three sets of notes and mark which beat produced the most useful line.
Note which beat you were tempted to skip, and do that one first tomorrow.
variations: Run the four beats at a place you visit often, and notice whether familiarity makes you skip the room or the groups.
Time each of the four beats for a few days, and notice which one you most often rush through.
Run the four beats before you walk into your own home after work, and notice what you see that you usually miss.

drills.name: Ground Up
steps: Sit somewhere you can see people standing or waiting, such as a bus stop or a queue.
Choose five people one at a time, never staring, and for each describe the feet, hands, torso, shoulders and head before looking at the face.
For each person, note whether the face and the lower body seemed to say the same thing.
Where they differed, write one ordinary explanation for the difference.
Stop if anyone notices you looking, and choose someone else.
variations: Practise ground-up reading on people in a film with the sound off, which removes any risk of staring at strangers.
Read one person you know well from the ground up, with their permission, and ask them afterwards whether your reading matched how they felt.
Notice your own feet and legs at the end of a meeting, and whether they were pointing at the door.

drills.name: Odd One Out
steps: In a busy place, run a quick scan and look only for the single most obvious exception: the still one, the one facing away, the one alone.
Note what made them stand out.
Without approaching or staring, watch for a minute to see whether an ordinary explanation appears.
Repeat twice more in different places.
Write down how many of the three exceptions turned out to need anything from anyone.
variations: Look for an exception that might need something other than help, such as someone who is simply enjoying being alone, and notice how you tell the difference.
Run the drill at a family gathering, and notice whether the exception you find is a person you would usually overlook.
Keep a tally over a week of how many exceptions needed anything at all, and notice whether your scans become calmer.

drills.name: Soft Eyes
steps: Sit facing a busy area and choose a fixed point slightly above eye level.
Keep your gaze relaxed on that point for two minutes, noticing movement at the edges.
Count how many people you can track by movement alone, and which way each is facing.
Practise glancing at one person for under a second and returning to your point.
Repeat until the glance and the return feel natural rather than furtive.
variations: Practise soft eyes while walking, keeping your gaze ahead and noticing how much of the street you can still take in.
Try the drill in a quieter place first, such as a library, before moving to a busier one.
Notice how other people manage civil inattention with you, and how brief their glances are.

quiz.q: In Simons and Chabris's experiment, roughly how many viewers counting basketball passes failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit?
options: Almost none
About half
Only those who were tired
Everyone
quiz.explain: About half missed it, because the counting task consumed the attention that would have noticed it. The lesson is not that those viewers were careless. It is that what you are looking for decides what reaches you, which is why a scan aims attention deliberately.

quiz.q: Why does the scan read each person from the ground up and leave the face for last?
options: Faces are less important than bodies, since most of what people feel is shown below the neck
It is faster, because feet and legs change less often and can be checked at a single glance
The lower body is less managed, and faces grab attention so readily that starting there crowds out the rest
People cannot see you looking at their feet, so it lets you watch them without being noticed
quiz.explain: Two reasons combine: the gradient of control from the leakage chapter, and the way faces pull and hold attention. Ending with the face means the rest of the body actually gets looked at. None of this makes the lower body a lie detector.

quiz.q: You arrive at a family barbecue. Running the scan, you notice your cousin at the far side of the garden, turned away from the group with arms folded, looking at his phone. What is the best output of the scan?
options: One small action: go and stand near him for a minute and see whether he wants company
Conclude that he is upset with someone at the party, and quietly ask the others who
Keep watching him for the rest of the afternoon until you can tell what is wrong
Tell the rest of the family he seems unhappy, so that someone can go and check on him
quiz.explain: The scan ends in a single question or action, then stops. Standing nearby offers company without demanding an explanation, and lets him tell you whether he wanted to be alone. Watching him all afternoon turns perception into surveillance.

quiz.q: What does Erving Goffman's term civil inattention describe?
options: Ignoring people you dislike, so politely that they can never quite be sure they are being ignored
Paying close attention to strangers in public places, for the sake of your own safety
Avoiding eye contact with strangers out of shyness, or a fear of being drawn into talk
The brief glance that acknowledges a stranger, followed by a polite withdrawal of attention
quiz.explain: Civil inattention is the everyday courtesy of public life: notice, then release. A good scan stays inside it. Staring breaks it, and people feel the break at once.

quiz.q: Is a longer, continuous scan of a room always better than a short one?
options: Yes, because more observation always means more information, and more information means better readings
No: a constant scan is vigilance, which tires you, unsettles others and narrows into threat-seeking
Yes, as long as you use soft eyes and keep moving your gaze so that nobody notices you
Only in professional settings, such as security work, where watching is part of the job
quiz.explain: The scan has an end so that you can be present with the people in the room. Continuous sweeping is a state of alarm, not a higher form of perception. If you cannot stop scanning, that tells you something about your own state.

quiz.q: A friend tells you, with some pride, that he can pick out easy targets in a bar from the way they walk. What does this chapter say about that skill?
options: It is a useful safety skill that everyone should learn, so that they can avoid looking like a target
It shows he has mastered the scan, since he can read a whole room from movement alone
The same looking can find who needs help or who could be exploited; this book teaches only the first
It is harmless as long as he never acts on it, since looking at people is not a crime
quiz.explain: Research on how assailants choose victims is a warning about what scanning can be used for, not a technique to copy. The scan in this book ends with the question of who could use something from you. If it ends with who would be easy, it has become something else.

quiz.q: In Anne Treisman's work on attention, which kind of item seems to pop out of a scene without effort?
options: An item defined by a particular combination of several different features
A single item that differs from everything around it in one simple feature
An item that is placed at the very centre of the scene, whatever it looks like
An item that the viewer has been told about in advance by the researchers
quiz.explain: A single item that differs in one simple feature, such as a red dot among green ones, pops out, while items defined by combinations of features need slow search. Rooms work similarly: the still person in a moving crowd stands out.

quiz.q: On playground duty, a teacher sees a boy with a calm face chatting to a friend, but his feet and body are turned towards the gate and he keeps glancing at the road. What fits this chapter best?
options: Read him as fine, since his calm face is the clearest sign of how he feels
Treat the difference as a question, and sit nearby to ask an ordinary question
Tell him firmly to move away from the gate, since he is clearly planning to leave
Call his parents straight away, since a child watching the road is always at risk
quiz.explain: Faces are the most managed part of the body; feet and orientation are among the least. When they disagree, the difference is a question worth asking, gently, with a small action that costs nothing if all is well.

quiz.q: Someone says peripheral vision is useless for reading people, so you have to look straight at each person. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That peripheral vision is poor at detail but good at movement and orientation, which is most of a scan
That peripheral vision is better at detail than central vision, so you never need to look directly at anyone
That peripheral vision only works in bright light, so it is no use in most rooms where people gather
That peripheral vision is only useful for spotting threats, and tells you nothing about anyone's mood
quiz.explain: Soft eyes rest lightly on a point and take in motion and orientation at the edges of vision, which is most of what a scan needs, while honouring civil inattention. A hard, fixed stare is both less effective and more intrusive.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific room you were in during the past month where you later learned something about someone that had been visible at the time and that you missed: a friend who was struggling, a colleague who was left out, someone who wanted to leave. Describe where your attention went instead. Then describe what a deliberate minute of looking, in the four beats, might have shown you, and what you could have done with it.
reflection.guidance: Be concrete about where your attention actually went: the person you were trying to impress, the argument you were following, your own phone. There is no blame in this; attention goes where our interests send it. The useful part is the second half, where you rebuild the room beat by beat. Most people find that the thing they missed was not hidden at all, only outside the narrow beam of what they were looking for, which is exactly what a routine scan is designed to widen.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to turn the scan into a performance of perceptiveness. The reader sweeps every room he enters, announces his readings to whoever is nearby, and treats the exceptions he spots as discoveries rather than questions. He stares, breaks civil inattention, and changes the very behaviour he thinks he is reading. A quieter failure is the scan that never ends: a man who keeps sweeping a party all night has not become more observant, only more vigilant, and the people around him can feel it. A third failure is looking only for exceptions that interest him and skipping the ones that would ask something of him. Keep it short, keep it in order, end it with a single question about who might need something, and then put it down and join the room.

moreCases.title: The waiter counting covers
moreCases.scene:
Rafael, twenty-six, is a waiter at a busy restaurant, and on Friday nights he works the main floor alone for the first hour. His manager has asked him to keep count of covers and table turns, because the kitchen is struggling. Rafael is good at it. He sweeps the room every few minutes, counting who is seated, who is waiting for a menu, who has finished and who has asked for the bill.

At half past seven, he is in the middle of a count when Mrs Ferreira, eighty-two, a regular who comes in every Friday, arrives at the door. She uses a walking frame, and the restaurant is crowded. She stands by the door for several minutes, unable to get through the gap between two tables to her usual seat by the window. Rafael passes within two metres of her three times. Each time he is counting, and each time he does not see her.

Eventually a customer at a nearby table stands up, helps her through and pulls out a chair. Mrs Ferreira sits down, upset, and when Rafael arrives with a menu she says quietly that she had thought he was ignoring her.

Rafael is mortified. He had been looking at the room the whole time. He tells his manager afterwards that he did not see her, and his manager does not quite believe him.

He had also, earlier that evening, failed to notice a child's spilled drink spreading across the floor by table six until he slipped in it. He had put it down to being busy.

He also realises, later, that the counting had felt like attention, which is why he had been so sure he was watching the whole room.
moreCases.misread:
Mrs Ferreira read Rafael's passing her three times as deliberate neglect, and his manager read his account as an excuse. Rafael read his own failure as carelessness, when he had been doing exactly what he was asked.

The customer who helped Mrs Ferreira through read Rafael as an indifferent young waiter, and left a review saying so.

And Rafael's manager read the miss as a lack of care, when it was the predictable result of the task he himself had set, done well.
moreCases.betterRead:
Simons and Chabris found that about half of the viewers counting basketball passes never saw a person in a gorilla suit walk through the game. The task consumed the attention that would have noticed the gorilla. Rafael's counting was such a task, and Mrs Ferreira, standing still in a moving room, was the exception that the scan in this chapter is designed to find. The better approach was to separate the two jobs. Rafael kept counting covers, but at each pass through the room he added one beat without a task: soft eyes, a sweep for anyone who stood apart from the pattern, and one question about who might need something. He also asked the manager to keep a gap clear by the door. The following Friday, he saw Mrs Ferreira before she was through it, and her usual table was ready.

Mrs Ferreira, the following week, told him that he had been the first waiter in years to have her table ready before she asked.

moreCases.title: The guard who stared
moreCases.scene:
Barry, fifty-two, is a security guard at a shopping centre, and he prides himself on noticing things. He stands near the main entrance and watches everyone who comes in, hard and steadily. When a group of teenagers arrives, he fixes on them, follows them with his eyes as they cross the atrium and keeps watching after they have gone into a shop.

The teenagers notice. They start to play up to it, walking slowly past him, staring back, laughing. One of them, a boy of fifteen, Kai, asks him what his problem is. Barry tells him to move along. The boy's friends film it. Within a week, the clip has been shared around the local school, and the shopping centre's manager, Joanne, receives two complaints from parents saying that their children are being treated like criminals.

Joanne watches the CCTV from the afternoon. In two hours, Barry looked at the teenagers for nearly forty minutes in total. In the same two hours, a man who was later reported for taking a woman's purse from her bag in the café walked past Barry twice, unwatched.

She asks Barry to come and see her.

Barry has also, over the years, been praised by managers for his alertness, and has come to believe that watching hard is the same as watching well.

Joanne also notices, on the footage, that every time Barry stares, the teenagers slow down and look back at him, which makes them look more suspicious to anyone watching the screen.
moreCases.misread:
Barry read his steady, hard watching of the teenagers as vigilance and good security. The teenagers read it as an accusation and responded to it, so that their behaviour began to confirm the suspicion that had caused it.

The parents who complained read the clip as evidence of a guard who disliked young people, which was partly right, and missed that he had simply been taught to stare.

Barry's previous managers had read his staring as diligence, and praised it, which is how the habit had grown.
moreCases.betterRead:
Goffman described civil inattention: the brief glance that acknowledges a stranger, followed by a withdrawal of attention that signals they are not an object of special interest. Barry's stare broke it, and broke it at a group of children, which changed the behaviour he thought he was reading. This chapter also describes how a hard, fixed stare is less effective than soft eyes, a relaxed gaze that takes in movement and orientation at the edges of vision: by fixing on the teenagers, Barry missed the man in the café. Joanne's better approach, which she trained into the team, was the scan as this chapter describes it: short sweeps in a fixed order, soft eyes, brief glances at individuals, and action only on specific behaviour. Barry was sceptical at first. Within a month, he had stopped two thefts, and the complaints from parents had stopped too.

Barry also started saying hello to the teenagers who came in regularly, with a nod and a brief glance, which they returned.

moreCases.title: The host who never stopped scanning
moreCases.scene:
Ross, thirty-seven, is hosting a fortieth birthday party for his wife, Fiona, in their house: forty guests, music in the kitchen, the garden lit with lanterns. He wants it to go perfectly, and he has read the earlier sections of this chapter. All evening, he scans. He stands in doorways and sweeps the room. He checks who is on their own, who has an empty glass, who is near the door, which groups are tight and which are drifting. He moves from room to room doing it.

He is very good at spotting things. He refills glasses, rescues a shy neighbour from a corner and introduces two people who turn out to get on well. But he barely talks to anyone for longer than a minute, and by eleven o'clock several guests have remarked to Fiona that Ross seems on edge. His oldest friend, Dougie, tries three times to have a proper conversation with him, and each time Ross's eyes drift over Dougie's shoulder to the room.

After the guests have gone, Fiona says, gently, that it felt as though he had been working the party rather than at it. She also says that she missed him.

Ross is tired in a way he does not understand, and slightly hurt. He had been trying to make it perfect for her.

He also, at one point, interrupts Fiona's sister mid-story to go and rescue a guest from a corner, and does not notice the look on her face as he leaves.
moreCases.misread:
Ross read his constant scanning as good hosting and his catches as proof that it was working. His guests, and Dougie in particular, read his drifting eyes as distraction and nerves, and felt that he was not quite with them.

And Ross read his own tiredness, at the end of the night, as the ordinary exhaustion of a host, when it was the cost of four hours of vigilance.
moreCases.betterRead: This chapter describes the scan as having an output and an end: a single question or small action, and then you stop and join the room. A scan that never ends is not perception but vigilance, tiring for the scanner and unsettling for the people around him. Ross's catches were real, but each one cost him a conversation, and the cumulative effect was a host who was everywhere and nowhere. The better approach, for the next party, was to run the scan once at the start and then once every half hour or so, as the observation in this chapter suggests, and between scans to stay in one conversation at a time. He also asked his sister to keep an eye on glasses and the shy neighbour, so that he did not have to. At Dougie's fiftieth, a year later, he spent forty minutes talking to the same three people, and Fiona said it was the best party he had ever been to.

moreCases.title: The boy at the gate
moreCases.scene:
Bethan, twenty-nine, is a primary school teacher, and on Wednesdays she is on playground duty at lunchtime. Like most of her colleagues, she reads the playground by faces: who is laughing, who is crying, who looks cross. One Wednesday, she notices Leo, eight, sitting on a bench near the school gate. His face is calm. He is chatting to a friend. She reads him as fine and moves on.

A few minutes later she happens to glance back and, without quite knowing why, looks at him again from the ground up, as she has read in this chapter. His feet are both pointed at the gate, his body is turned slightly towards it, one hand is gripping the edge of the bench, and he keeps glancing past his friend at the road. His face is still calm.

She walks over, sits on the end of the bench and asks Leo and his friend what they are talking about. Leo says football. Then he says, without being asked, that his mum said she might come and get him at lunch because his nan is in hospital, and that he is waiting to see if she comes.

Bethan says that she will check with the office, and that if his mum comes, someone will come and find him straight away.

Her colleague on the other side of the playground, asked later, says that she had seen Leo too, and had thought he looked perfectly happy.

She also notices that Leo's school bag is beside him on the bench, packed and zipped, at the start of lunch, which no other child's is.
moreCases.misread:
Bethan's first reading, from Leo's calm face and his chat with a friend, was that he was fine. The rest of his body, which she had not looked at, was oriented entirely towards the gate and the road.

Leo's friend, sitting beside him, had read him as fine too, because Leo had been working hard to seem it.

Leo, too, had read the adults around him as unlikely to help, and had decided to wait at the gate on his own rather than ask anyone.
moreCases.betterRead:
This chapter explains why the scan reads each person from the ground up and leaves the face for last: the feet and legs are among the least managed parts of the body and the face the most, and faces capture attention so readily that they tend to hold you. Leo's face was managed, as children's often are with adults, and his feet, his torso and his grip on the bench told the truer story. The better reading treated the orientation as a question rather than a verdict: it might have meant nothing, or a plan to slip out, or a worry. Sitting down and asking an ordinary question was the small action. The office confirmed that his mother was on her way, and Bethan walked Leo to reception when she arrived. Afterwards, she started reading the playground from the ground up, and noticed two more children that term who were waiting for something.

She also mentioned the pattern to her colleagues at the next staff meeting, without naming Leo, and two of them started reading the playground the same way.

workedReading.title: Running the scan at a wake
workedReading.scene:
Alun, fifty-five, has driven three hours to the wake for his oldest friend, Gwyn, who died suddenly last week. The wake is in a rugby club function room, crowded, warm and loud, with a bar along one wall and doors open to a car park where some people have gone to smoke. Alun knows Gwyn's wife, Sian, and their two children well, and very few of the other hundred people there. He is grieving, and he wants to be useful rather than in the way. As he stands in the doorway, he decides to run the sixty-second scan in its four beats before he goes in, and then to stop, because he does not want to spend his friend's wake watching people.

He also knows that wakes can be hard places to read, because grief makes some people loud and others very still, and he reminds himself that most of what he sees will be ordinary mourning, not anything that needs him.

steps.label: Yourself first
steps.text:
He notices that his jaw is tight, his breathing is high and his shoulders are up. He is tired from the drive and close to tears. He wants, more than anything, to find Sian and do something. He breathes out slowly once. The first beat matters, as the first chapter of this part explained: his state will colour everything he sees, and he wants to know it is there before he starts reading anyone.

He also notes, honestly, that he wants to be needed, and that this may make him see need where there is none.

steps.label: The room
steps.text:
He takes in the room: the bar on the left with a crowd three deep, the buffet table at the far end, a slideshow of photographs on a screen near the window, the open doors to the car park, and the noise, which is loud enough that people are leaning in to talk. He notes that the room is pushing people into clusters by the bar and the buffet, and leaving the corners by the screen nearly empty.

He also notices that the open doors to the car park are where people go to be alone for a minute, and that this is part of how the room works.

steps.label: The groups
steps.text:
He looks at the groups with soft eyes, not fixing on anyone. Gwyn's rugby friends are in a tight knot by the bar. Sian is in the middle of the room, surrounded, receiving a stream of people. Several older relatives are seated along one wall. A group of teenagers, friends of Gwyn's children, are by the buffet. Most groups face inwards. He does all this in about fifteen seconds, with brief glances, so that nobody feels watched.

He also notices that Gwyn's daughter is with her friends by the buffet, laughing, and reads it as ordinary grief, not as anything wrong.

steps.label: One person, from the ground up
steps.text:
One figure stands apart: Gwyn's son, Rhys, sixteen, by the screen, alone, watching the slideshow. Alun looks at him from the ground up. His feet are together, pointed at the screen; his hands are pushed deep in his pockets; his shoulders are raised and his head is down. His face, when he glances round at the room, is composed. The rest of him is not.

He resists the urge to keep looking. A second glance would have been enough; a third would have been staring.

He also notes that Rhys is standing where he can see the door, as if ready to leave, which adds to the question rather than answering it.

steps.label: The exception as a question
steps.text:
Alun does not conclude anything. Rhys might want to be alone, which would be perfectly reasonable. He might be avoiding the crowd. He might be close to breaking down. The scan has found an exception, and the chapter is clear that an exception is a question, not a discovery. Alun's question is simple: is Rhys on his own because he wants to be?

He also reminds himself that if Rhys wants to be alone, the kindest thing will be to leave him there.

He also checks his own state again: the urge to be useful is strong, and he reminds himself that his question is about Rhys, not about his own need to help.

steps.label: One small action
steps.text:
He gets two glasses of water from the bar and walks over to the screen, slowly, stopping a little to the side of Rhys rather than in front of him, so that they are both facing the photographs. He offers a glass and says, "That's your dad at my wedding. He lost the rings." Rhys laughs, takes the water, and after a minute says that he cannot face talking to anyone else today. Alun says he does not have to, and stays, side by side, looking at the photographs, saying very little.

He also does not ask Rhys how he is feeling, which, he suspects, Rhys has been asked fifty times that day.

steps.label: Stop scanning, and be there
steps.text:
After twenty minutes Rhys goes to find his sister, and Alun goes to find Sian. He does not run the scan again for the rest of the afternoon. He talks to Gwyn's rugby friends, tells two stories, cries once in the car park, and leaves at six. Sian rings him a week later to say that Rhys had told her Alun was the only person at the wake who did not ask him how he was feeling.

He also notices, driving home, that he feels he was at the wake rather than watching it, which was what he had wanted.

moreFailures.title: Scanning only for threat
moreFailures.body:
When people learn to scan, many start looking mainly for danger: the person who seems agitated, the group that might cause trouble, the stranger who does not fit. Some of that is sensible, especially in jobs such as security. But a scan aimed only at threat narrows quickly, and it misses most of what the scan in this chapter is meant to find: the person who is lost, alone, unwell, upset or waiting for something, as Leo was at the gate and Mrs Ferreira was at the restaurant door. A threat-only scan also tends to land on the same kinds of people over and over, often young men, often from particular backgrounds, as Barry's did, and breaks civil inattention with exactly the people least likely to be doing anything wrong. End every scan with the question this chapter recommends: who here might need something? Threat is one possible answer among many.

It also helps to notice whose behaviour you most often read as threatening, and whether the pattern is about them or about you.

A threat-only scan also wears out the scanner faster, because it keeps the body braced for something that rarely comes.

moreFailures.title: Using the scan to find the vulnerable for the wrong reasons
moreFailures.body:
The ability to sweep a room and pick out the person who stands apart is not morally neutral, as this chapter says plainly. Grayson and Stein's study, often cited in self-defence courses, found that people judged by others to be easy targets moved in recognisable ways. Some readers will notice that the same skill could be used to find people to exploit: the lonely customer who can be sold to, the newcomer who can be pressured, the person who will not complain. This book does not teach that, and the scan is not for it. The ethics chapter in this part sets out the line: reading is for understanding and helping, never for steering people against their interests. If you notice that your scans are increasingly aimed at finding people who are easy to influence, stop, and ask what you are using the skill for.

A simple test is to ask whether the person you have noticed would thank you for what you plan to do. If not, do not do it.

moreFailures.title: Skipping yourself
moreFailures.body:
The first beat of the scan, yourself, is the one people most often skip, because it feels like a delay before the interesting part. It is not a delay. Your state colours everything that follows: a man who walks into a room tired and braced will read tension in the groups that a rested man would read as ordinary chat, and a man who wants a deal to close will read warmth in a client who is simply being polite. The first chapter of this part makes the same point for the journal. Fifteen seconds is enough: breath, shoulders, jaw, and one honest answer to the question of what you want from this room. Alun noticed that he was close to tears before he looked at anyone, which let him read Rhys more gently. If you skip the first beat, every later beat carries your state without your knowing.

It is also worth noticing whether your state changes the kind of exception you find: tired scans tend to find threats, hopeful ones find warmth.

moreFailures.title: Mistaking the room for the person
moreFailures.body:
The second beat of the scan, the room, often explains more behaviour than any person does. A cold office keeps arms folded; a loud bar makes everyone lean in close; a narrow hallway crowds bodies together; a slideshow of a dead friend makes people stand still and quiet. Readers who skip the room, or rush it, tend to attribute to people what belongs to the setting: reading folded arms in a draughty meeting room as defensiveness, or closeness in a noisy pub as intimacy. Before you read any person, ask what the room is doing to everyone in it. If most people share a behaviour, it is probably the room. The exception worth noticing is the person who differs from what the room is pushing everyone else to do, not the person who is simply doing what the room demands.

A good habit is to ask, before reading any person, what you would be doing in their place in this particular room.

questions.q: Won't people notice me scanning them?
questions.a:
Not if you do it as this chapter describes. A scan done with soft eyes, a relaxed gaze resting lightly on a point and taking in movement and orientation at the edges of vision, is almost invisible. When you need to look at an individual, a glance of under a second, followed by a return to your resting point, is the brief acknowledgement Goffman called civil inattention, which strangers extend to each other all the time. What people do notice is a hard, fixed stare, a head that swivels to follow them, or eyes that keep drifting over someone's shoulder during a conversation, as Ross's did. The Soft Eyes drill practises the glance and the return. If anyone notices you looking, look away, and choose someone else, or stop.

It also helps to scan from a natural position, such as a doorway or a seat, rather than from the middle of a room where your eyes are more noticeable.

questions.q: How do I stop scanning once I have started?
questions.a:
By giving the scan an end. This chapter's rule is that every scan produces one question or one small action, and then stops: you put it down and join the room. Tie it to transitions, such as walking into a room or sitting down, so that it happens at natural moments rather than continuously. At a long event, a scan every half hour is plenty. If you find that you cannot stop scanning, that you sweep every room for threats, cannot relax in crowds and feel constantly on alert, that may be a sign of something more than a habit. People who have been through trauma or long periods of stress sometimes find themselves stuck in this state, and it is worth talking to your GP, who can help you find support.

It can also help to put the scan down deliberately, with a small physical signal to yourself such as sitting down or picking up a drink.

questions.q: What should I do if the scan finds someone who seems to need help?
questions.a:
Start with the smallest, lowest-key action that would help if they need it and cost nothing if they do not. Treat what you have noticed as a question, not a conclusion, as Joe did with Theo, Bethan with Leo and Alun with Rhys. Often the best action is to make yourself available without making them the centre of attention: give them a job, offer a drink, sit beside them, ask an ordinary question. Avoid asking "What's wrong?" or "Are you OK?" in front of others, which puts people on the spot. If the person is a child, tell the adult responsible. If someone is in danger or in a medical emergency, get help at once. And if they make it clear they want to be left alone, respect it.

Afterwards, resist the urge to tell others what you noticed. The person you helped may not want it known.

And if your action turns out to be unnecessary, that is fine. A friendly word costs nothing and is rarely unwelcome.

questions.q: Does the scan work on video calls?
questions.a:
In an adapted form. The yourself beat is the same: notice your own state before the call starts. The room becomes the call itself: how many people, who has video on, how good the connection is, whether there is a delay. The groups become the patterns of who talks to whom and who reacts to whom. And the exception is often easier to spot on a gallery view: the one person with the camera off, the one who has not spoken, the one whose face has gone still while everyone else is nodding. The chapters on video calls in Part IV explain how much the camera distorts, so hold readings even more lightly. End the scan, as always, with one question, such as whether to ask the quiet person for their view, and then get on with the call.

It also helps to scan at the start of the call, before the agenda takes over, since that is when the task-free beat is easiest.

questions.q: Why start with the feet rather than the face?
questions.a:
For two reasons, both described in this chapter. The first is the gradient of control: most people manage their faces carefully and their feet and legs hardly at all, so the lower body gives you the less curated signal first, as Leo's feet did at the gate. The second is that faces capture attention more readily than almost anything else in a scene; if you start with a face, it tends to hold you, and you may never look at the rest. Reading from the ground up corrects for both. It does not mean that feet are more truthful than faces in some absolute sense. Often the two agree. When they disagree, the disagreement is the thing worth noticing, and the question worth asking.

It also helps to notice whether you were drawn to the face before you had finished the sweep, which happens to almost everyone at first.

questions.q: Can I train myself to stop missing things like the gorilla?
questions.a:
Not entirely, and it would not help if you could. Inattentional blindness is a consequence of attention itself: when you focus on a task, you stop noticing what the task does not need. Nobody can attend to everything at once. What you can do is choose your tasks deliberately, and build in moments without a task, as the Count and Miss drill demonstrates: a second look at a scene with no counting, no searching, just taking it in. The scan's fixed order works in the same way: by moving through the beats, you give your attention a series of small, different tasks rather than one large one. Rafael did not stop counting covers; he added a beat in which he was not counting anything.

It also helps to accept that you will always miss something, and to build habits, such as a second look, that catch the important misses.

watch.title: An FBI Expert's Simplest Rule for Reading People
watch.notice: A short clip on a simple rule for reading people. Compare it with the sixty-second scan: what to look at first, and what to leave until you know more.

reviewPrompt: The next time you enter a room with at least five people in it, run the four-beat scan in under a minute and then stop. Afterwards, write one line about the one thing you would have missed without it.
